Point liveness at /ready, stop Redis, and Kubernetes restarts every pod over and over — restarts can't fix Redis, and the restart storm makes recovery slower. Liveness checks only the process itself. Never check the model API in any probe either: one slow provider would take your whole service out.

On delete: → the pod is removed from endpoints, and the preStop hook runs (sleep 5 s: let every proxy notice) → SIGTERM: uvicorn stops accepting, FINISHES in-flight requests, exits → after terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30 s here), SIGKILL A slow LLM request started before the delete still completes. With a 1-second grace period it's cut off. For long streams raise terminationGracePeriodSeconds (and the platform's equivalent, below).

Under memory pressure, BestEffort pods are evicted first, Guaranteed last.

On real clusters, teams start from a namespace-wide default-deny and then allow each flow (plus DNS). (kind's simple network plugin also drops REPLY traffic to default-denied pods, so this lesson keeps to the Redis policy; Cilium or Calico, used by the clouds, track connections properly.)

lesson_title: The front door: Gateway API routes outside traffic to your Services (and the 15-second trap)
text: One entry point for the whole cluster: a load balancer → a gateway proxy (Envoy) → routes by host and path → Services. Kubernetes' API for this is the Gateway API (GA since 2023). The older `Ingress` API still works, but ingress-nginx, its most used controller, was RETIRED in March 2026 (no more fixes): new setups use a Gateway API implementation. Here: Envoy Gateway, installed with one `kubectl apply`.

lesson_title: The front door: Gateway API routes outside traffic to your Services (and the 15-second trap)
text: Who owns what:  GatewayClass (which controller; the platform team)  →  Gateway (the listener: port 80, which namespaces may attach; the platform team)  →  HTTPRoute (host/path → Service; each app team, in its namespace). kind maps 127.0.0.1:6580 to the gateway's node port, so the gateway is reachable from your laptop.

lesson_title: Autoscaling: more pods when busy, fewer when quiet — and why CPU is the wrong signal for LLM apps
text: metrics-server collects CPU and memory per pod (every 15 s). A HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA) compares them with a target — "average CPU = 50% of the request" — and changes the Deployment's replica count: desired = ceil(current replicas × current utilization / target) It needs CPU REQUESTS on the pods (utilization is a percentage of the request).

lesson_title: Autoscaling: more pods when busy, fewer when quiet — and why CPU is the wrong signal for LLM apps
text: `behavior` controls the pace: scale up fast, scale down slowly (default: wait 5 minutes of lower load, so a short dip doesn't throw away capacity you'll need again). This lesson shortens scale-down to 30 s to watch it.

lesson_title: Autoscaling: more pods when busy, fewer when quiet — and why CPU is the wrong signal for LLM apps

lesson_title: Autoscaling: more pods when busy, fewer when quiet — and why CPU is the wrong signal for LLM apps

Scale an LLM service on what it actually runs out of: in-flight requests / concurrency    Cloud Run and Container Apps do this natively (--concurrency, http scale rule) queue length                        KEDA (for workers, lesson 11) custom metrics (Prometheus)         KEDA or prometheus-adapter: e.g. nimbus_requests_in_flight per pod And remember the real ceiling is usually the PROVIDER's rate limit, not your pods (Production course lesson 9).

lesson_title: Rolling updates and rollbacks: ship a new version with zero failed requests, and undo a bad one
text: Changing the image (`kubectl set image`, or a new tag in the overlay) starts a rolling update: new pods start, become READY, receive traffic; old pods drain and stop — a few at a time: maxSurge: 1          at most 1 pod above the desired count during the update maxUnavailable: 0    never fewer ready pods than desired (capacity never dips) Readiness probes + preStop + graceful shutdown (lesson 7) are what make it zero-downtime. Traffic runs through the gateway the whole time; we count every answer by version.

lesson_title: Rolling updates and rollbacks: ship a new version with zero failed requests, and undo a bad one
text: Each change is a revision: `kubectl rollout history`. The Deployment keeps old ReplicaSets (scaled to 0) so it can go back instantly.

lesson_title: Rolling updates and rollbacks: ship a new version with zero failed requests, and undo a bad one
text: A bad release (1.2.0 shipped with a wrong Redis host): its first pod never becomes ready, so the rollout STOPS there — maxUnavailable: 0 keeps every old pod serving. Users notice nothing; `rollout status` times out. (`progressDeadlineSeconds` then marks the Deployment as failed — that's what CI should alert on.)

lesson_title: Rolling updates and rollbacks: ship a new version with zero failed requests, and undo a bad one
text: `kubectl rollout undo` → back to the previous revision in seconds, no rebuild. Then fix forward.

lesson_title: Rolling updates and rollbacks: ship a new version with zero failed requests, and undo a bad one
text: Node maintenance: `kubectl drain` evicts pods so a node can be upgraded. A PodDisruptionBudget (minAvailable: 1) makes evictions wait so the API never drops below one ready pod. Too strict a budget (minAvailable = replicas) blocks the drain completely — and with it every node upgrade. Evicted pods shut down like any other: without the preStop sleep (lesson 7), this drain produced a few 503s — the gateway still sent requests to pods that had already exited.

lesson_title: Canary and blue/green releases: expose a new version to a few requests first, or switch all at once
text: Canary: run the new version NEXT TO the old one (two Deployments, two Services) and let the gateway split traffic by weight — HTTPRoute backendRefs with weight 90 / 10. A header rule sends testers (`x-canary: true`) to the new version every time.

lesson_title: Canary and blue/green releases: expose a new version to a few requests first, or switch all at once
text: Promote step by step: 10% → 50% → 100%, watching errors and latency at each step. Then the old Deployment can go.

lesson_title: Canary and blue/green releases: expose a new version to a few requests first, or switch all at once
text: An automated gate: a bad canary gets 10% of traffic. It passes its health checks — /health and /ready are fine — but it shipped with a 10 ms model timeout, so every question fails with 504. The gate measures the error rate on real requests, sees it above 1%, and sets the canary's weight back to 0. Health checks can't catch a broken feature; only request metrics can. (A canary that never becomes READY gets no traffic at all: the gateway skips backends without ready pods.) Tools that do this for you: Argo Rollouts or Flagger (Kubernetes, with Prometheus metrics), ECS native canary with CloudWatch alarms, Cloud Deploy for Cloud Run.

lesson_title: Canary and blue/green releases: expose a new version to a few requests first, or switch all at once
text: Blue/green: two FULL environments; the live Service's selector points at one (`track: blue`). Switching is one change and instant, and switching back is just as fast. Costs double capacity while both run.

lesson_title: Canary and blue/green releases: expose a new version to a few requests first, or switch all at once
text: Which to use: canary limits the blast radius (and needs good metrics); blue/green gives instant, all-or-nothing switches (good for a release that must not mix versions). Weights are PER REQUEST: one user can bounce between versions. For chat UIs, route by user instead — a header/cookie rule, or app-level flags like the Production course's prompt canary (lesson 16), which hashes the caller id.

lesson_title: Caching in depth: exact, semantic and embedding caches
text: Why cache an LLM app: latency, cost and the provider's rate-limit budget; measured as hit rate, false-hit rate, latency saved and tokens/$ saved.

lesson_title: Caching in depth: exact, semantic and embedding caches
text: Exact-match cache key: a hash of the normalized prompt + model + settings; normalization (case, whitespace, punctuation) raises the hit rate without wrong answers.

lesson_title: Caching in depth: exact, semantic and embedding caches
text: Semantic cache lookup: embed the question, find the nearest cached question, and reuse its answer when the similarity is above a threshold.

lesson_title: Caching in depth: exact, semantic and embedding caches
text: What a semantic cache entry stores: question text, its embedding, the answer, model, prompt version, index version, sources, tenant/scope, created_at, TTL and hit count.

lesson_title: Caching in depth: exact, semantic and embedding caches
text: Choosing the similarity threshold from data: paraphrase pairs (should hit) vs near-miss pairs (must not hit), precision and false hits at each threshold.

lesson_title: Caching in depth: exact, semantic and embedding caches
text: Near-miss protection: an entity guard so numbers, IDs, dates and names in the question must match before a cached answer is reused.

lesson_title: Caching in depth: exact, semantic and embedding caches
text: Storage backends: in-memory, SQLite, PostgreSQL + pgvector and Redis (vector search) run and compared on lookup latency, persistence, TTL support and operating cost.

lesson_title: Caching in depth: exact, semantic and embedding caches
text: What to cache: FAQ-style answers, retrieval results, embeddings (CacheBackedEmbeddings), reranker scores and slow tool results.

lesson_title: Caching in depth: exact, semantic and embedding caches
text: What never to cache: personalised or permission-dependent answers, time-sensitive data, actions with side effects, errors, refusals and low-confidence answers.

lesson_title: Caching in depth: exact, semantic and embedding caches
text: Invalidation: TTLs, version keys (model, prompt version, index version) so re-ingesting changed documents retires stale answers, and explicit purge on source change.

lesson_title: Caching in depth: exact, semantic and embedding caches
text: Scoping and safety: separate caches per tenant, user group, language and access rights; personal data in cache entries; cache poisoning.

text: Provider prompt caching (repeated prompt prefixes billed cheaper) vs response caching: different mechanisms, often used together.

lesson_title: Caching in depth: exact, semantic and embedding caches

lesson_title: Retrieval metrics in depth: hit, precision, recall, nDCG, MAP, F1 and MRR

lesson_title: Retrieval metrics in depth: hit, precision, recall, nDCG, MAP, F1 and MRR

lesson_title: Retrieval metrics in depth: hit, precision, recall, nDCG, MAP, F1 and MRR

text: nDCG@k: relevant chunks score more the higher they rank, divided by the score of the ideal ranking; the standard metric for comparing rankers and rerankers.

lesson_title: Retrieval metrics in depth: hit, precision, recall, nDCG, MAP, F1 and MRR

lesson_title: Retrieval metrics in depth: hit, precision, recall, nDCG, MAP, F1 and MRR
